stories.headline: Golden fire department employee fired after hanging Black doll by neck in station stairwell
stories.summary:
The City of Golden has launched an independent investigation into the Golden Fire Department after an employee hung a Black novelty doll by a rope around its neck in a fire station stairwell in March 2026. The incident involved a "Snoop on a Stoop" doll — a parody of the "Elf on a Shelf" toy modeled after Snoop Dogg — that had been moved around the fire station for an extended period during the holiday season before being found hanging by the neck.

Mayor Laura Weinberg read a prepared statement at Golden City Council on Tuesday calling the act "deeply disturbing and racist" and acknowledging that the city's initial internal response "did not adequately reflect the seriousness of this incident or the impact it had on our employees and community." The employee responsible has since been terminated, and an outside consultant had previously been hired to develop diversity, equity, and inclusion training for the department.

City Manager Scott Vargo, who originally agreed to an interview with Denver7 before canceling, acknowledged in an internal email obtained by the station that he "should have been transparent" about the incident sooner. A member of a task force designed to support diversity within Golden told Denver7 they were only notified this week about the March incident.

The announcement of an independent investigation came after Denver7 first reported on the incident following a tip from an anonymous source. The city faces scrutiny over its months-long delay in publicly addressing the matter.

stories.headline: RTD board votes 9-6 to advance $20 million in bus and rail service cuts for 2027
stories.summary:
The Regional Transportation District board voted 9-6 Tuesday night to move forward with recommending approximately $20 million in service cuts to the agency's bus and rail network, set to take effect in 2027. The decision came after months of review as RTD works to address a deficit exceeding $200 million.

Riders packed the meeting to urge board members to keep fares in place and preserve service, particularly for transit-dependent communities across the Denver metro area. The vote advances the cuts as a recommendation rather than a final decision, though it signals the board's direction as the agency grapples with its financial shortfall.

RTD has been examining multiple parts of its transit system as part of a broader effort to close the budget gap. The agency has faced ongoing criticism over reliability and ridership levels that have not fully recovered since the pandemic.

The approved cuts would affect both bus routes and rail service, though specific lines slated for reduction were not detailed in initial reports. The move is likely to renew debate about the long-term sustainability of public transit funding in the Denver metro region.

stories.headline: Democrats lay out 13-race strategy to win supermajorities in Colorado legislature
stories.summary:
The Democratic Legislative Campaign Committee announced Wednesday that its path to winning 2-to-1 supermajorities in both chambers of the Colorado General Assembly runs through 13 targeted House and Senate seats. Democrats currently hold 43 of 65 House seats and 23 of 35 Senate seats — one short of a supermajority in each chamber.

The DLCC is targeting eight House districts and five Senate districts, with a mix of offensive flips and defensive holds. Seats the party hopes to flip include House Districts 16 (Colorado Springs), 19 (Frederick), 50 (Fort Lupton), and 51 (Loveland), along with Senate District 30 in Highlands Ranch. Democrats also plan to defend seats in districts ranging from Conifer to Pueblo to Durango.

A supermajority would give Democrats the power to refer constitutional amendments to voters, override gubernatorial vetoes, and control committee makeup without any Republican support. Democrats previously held a House supermajority in 2022 and 2023 — the only time either party has achieved that status in either chamber since at least 1992.

DLCC support for targeted races will include polling, data and research, paid communications, and direct voter contact. The general election is set for Nov. 3.

stories.headline: Jeffco Public Schools sues Trump administration, asks court to clarify conflicting federal and state law
stories.summary:
Jefferson County Public Schools has filed a lawsuit against the Trump administration's Department of Education, asking a federal judge to determine which set of directives the district is legally required to follow after new federal guidelines were found to conflict with current Colorado law. The district says it is caught between competing legal obligations and cannot comply with both simultaneously.

Jeffco is not alone in facing federal pressure. The Education Department opened a separate investigation in June into Cherry Creek Schools over complaints that district programs and clubs discriminate against white students. Cherry Creek called the administration's claim a "factual misunderstanding" and said it has attempted to mediate the dispute in good faith.

The Trump administration has launched dozens of investigations into school districts nationwide over policies related to transgender and LGBTQ+ students, including a previous Title IX complaint against Denver Public Schools over bathroom access policies. The Jeffco lawsuit represents an escalation in the legal conflict between Colorado school districts and federal education authorities.

The outcome of the case could have implications for how Colorado districts navigate the growing tension between state civil rights protections and federal education policy directives under the current administration.

stories.headline: Federal investigators open probe into Denver Public Schools over allegation teacher required students to kiss
stories.summary:
The U.S. Department of Education announced Tuesday it is investigating Denver Public Schools over allegations that a high school teacher required students of the same sex to kiss in front of a class. The federal probe will determine whether DPS violated the Protection of Pupil Rights Amendment, a law giving parents the right to opt their children out of school evaluations or activities touching on sexual behavior or attitudes.

DPS spokesman Scott Pribble said the district placed the teacher on administrative leave and completed its own investigation after students raised concerns in March 2025. The Board of Education voted to fire the teacher in May. DPS did not specify whether its internal investigation substantiated the specific allegation cited by federal officials.

"The safety, emotional well-being, and dignity of our students are the absolute highest priorities of DPS," the district said in a statement, adding that its actions were "wholly consistent with those priorities." The Education Department also announced a simultaneous investigation into a Washington state district involving testosterone vials displayed during a Pride Month exhibit.

The investigations are part of a broader pattern of the Trump administration scrutinizing school districts in Democratic-led states. The administration has previously accused DPS of violating Title IX protections over bathroom policies for transgender students.

stories.headline: Denver City Council considers 'slavery acknowledgment' to be read at start of meetings
stories.summary:
The Denver City Council is debating a proposal to add a formal "slavery acknowledgment" to the opening of its meetings, recognizing the forced labor of enslaved Africans and the lasting legacy of slavery, segregation, and racial terror in the United States and Denver specifically. Councilwoman Shontel Lewis brought the proposal forward during a Finance and Business Committee meeting Tuesday.

The proposed text references the transatlantic slave trade, chattel slavery, Jim Crow laws, lynching, and the historic presence of Ku Klux Klan members among Denver government officials. It would be read alongside the existing land acknowledgment and the Pledge of Allegiance. The committee postponed a vote until next month after members debated whether the language was inclusive enough.

Council President Diana Romero-Campbell suggested the acknowledgment could be broadened to include other historically marginalized groups, such as migrant workers and Japanese Americans held in internment camps. Councilman Chris Hinds questioned whether singling out "White Americans" by name was the appropriate framing compared to referencing oppressive systems more broadly.

Lewis, who is also running for mayor, said the intent is to convert an acknowledgment of historic pain into policy that addresses ongoing suffering. The committee is expected to revisit the proposal next month.

stories.headline: Wildfire near Pagosa Springs grows to 440 acres, threatens 373 homes with mandatory evacuations underway
stories.summary:
A new wildfire broke out approximately 10 miles south of Pagosa Springs in Archuleta County on July 28, rapidly expanding from an initial estimate of 120 acres to roughly 440 acres by Wednesday morning, according to National Interagency Fire Center mapping. The Rio Grande Fire is fully uncontained and is threatening 373 homes in the area.

Mandatory evacuations are in effect for residents along CR 335 (Lower Blanco), while pre-evacuation orders have been issued for CR 337, CR 339, and the Pinon Hills area along CR 500. No structures had been confirmed lost as of the 7:30 a.m. update Wednesday, though the fire burned 50 yards into a neighborhood shortly after ignition. The cause has been reported as natural.

Firefighting efforts on Wednesday are focused on structure protection and establishing anchor points from which crews can safely conduct operations. Aviation resources were not available for mapping early Wednesday morning, creating some uncertainty in the size estimates.

Residents can track updates through the Archuleta County Sheriff's Office Facebook page or the Watch Duty app. The fire adds to an already active wildfire season across Colorado.

stories.headline: Flash flooding forces evacuations near Ouray, closes U.S. 550 and Red Mountain Pass
stories.summary:
Ouray County officials ordered evacuations Wednesday evening near the Gold Mountain burn scar as intense flash flooding struck the area, closing U.S. 550 and Red Mountain Pass in both directions. Residents near Ponderosa Village and Cutler Creek Drive, located between Ridgway and Ouray, were told to evacuate or move to high ground immediately due to "active intense flooding."

U.S. 550 was closed in both directions at Cutler Creek, approximately four miles north of Ouray, with no estimated reopening time. Red Mountain Pass between Ouray and Silverton was also shut down due to active flooding and severe road damage, according to the Colorado Department of Transportation.

Separately, flooding near the Aspen Acres burn scar closed roads in Beulah in Pueblo County on Wednesday night. The Beulah Fire Protection and Ambulance District reported multiple road closures due to water and debris, and a flash flood emergency had been declared earlier in the day for the burn scar area.

The closures are the latest in a series of flood events hitting Colorado this week as thunderstorms repeatedly strike areas already saturated or scarred by recent wildfires, creating hazardous runoff conditions.

stories.headline: Two killed in head-on crash near Dolores in southwestern Colorado
stories.summary:
Two drivers were killed Tuesday morning in a head-on collision near Dolores in Montezuma County, according to the Colorado State Patrol. The crash occurred around 8:30 a.m. near mile marker three on Colorado Highway 184, west of Dolores.

A Dodge pickup truck traveling east swerved into westbound lanes and struck a recreational vehicle head-on. State patrol officials said the Dodge had been reported to law enforcement prior to the crash for "weaving all over the roadway." Both the Dodge driver, an 84-year-old man, and the RV driver, a 49-year-old man, died at the scene.

The Montezuma County Coroner's Office will formally identify both victims. Colorado 184 was closed in both directions following the crash for cleanup and investigation but had fully reopened by Wednesday morning.

The crash adds to a series of fatal roadway incidents across Colorado this week as summer travel continues and weather conditions in parts of the state create additional hazards.

stories.headline: VF Corp. shares plunge 17% as CFO resigns amid quarterly loss and declining Vans sales
stories.summary:
Denver-based VF Corporation saw its stock fall 17% Wednesday after Chief Financial Officer Paul Vogel announced his resignation amid a quarterly earnings report that revealed continued losses and declining sales for the Vans brand. Chief Operating Officer Abhishek Dalmia will assume the CFO role as the company navigates its ongoing financial restructuring.

VF Corp., the parent company of outdoor and apparel brands including The North Face, Timberland, and Vans, has been working to stabilize its finances following years of debt accumulation and underperforming brands. The Vans line in particular has struggled to regain traction with consumers despite efforts to revamp the brand's marketing and product lineup.

The executive departure and weak quarterly results represent a setback for the company's turnaround efforts. VF Corp. has been shedding assets and cutting costs as it works to reduce its debt load, including the earlier sale of the Supreme streetwear brand.

The company remains headquartered in Denver, making its financial performance a significant concern for the local business community and its regional workforce.

stories.headline: Rockies prospect Charlie Condon on track for MLB debut in second half of season
stories.summary:
Colorado Rockies farm director Chris Forbes said Wednesday that top prospect Charlie Condon is on track to make his major league debut during the second half of the 2026 season. Condon, the No. 3 overall pick in the 2024 draft, is hitting .288 with a .406 on-base percentage and 20 home runs in 86 games for Triple-A Albuquerque.

The Rockies' 40-man roster is currently full, meaning the club would need to free up a spot — likely through a trade ahead of the Aug. 3 deadline — to call up the 23-year-old first baseman and corner outfielder. Corner outfielders Mickey Moniak and Troy Johnston have been identified as candidates to be dealt. Forbes said the front office is focused on navigating the trade deadline before determining the timeline for Condon's promotion.

Condon has overcome significant injury setbacks, including a bone spur on his right ring finger that hampered his debut pro season and a fractured left wrist that delayed the start of the 2025 campaign. Forbes praised Condon's consistency and composure, noting his ability to handle adversity at the plate as a sign of his readiness.

In other Rockies minor league news, the Arizona Complex League Rockies won the ACL Championship Series Tuesday, with 19-year-old Venezuelan outfielder Cristian Arguelles — who hit .402 during the regular season — earning promotion to Low-A Fresno.

stories.headline: Megan Moroney cancels Ball Arena show mid-performance due to illness; concert rescheduled for Aug. 27
stories.summary:
Country singer Megan Moroney abruptly canceled her Tuesday night concert at Ball Arena in Denver after performing just three songs, citing illness. Moroney addressed the crowd directly before leaving the stage, telling fans it was "the last thing I ever wanted to do" and that she was "obviously extremely sick."

In an Instagram story post following the cancellation, Moroney said she "never ever will give you guys a show that is not 100%" and described the decision as "the hardest I've ever had to make." She is currently touring in support of her February 2026 album "Cloud 9."

Ball Arena confirmed that all tickets purchased for the original date will be honored at a rescheduled performance on Aug. 27. Fans unable to attend the new date are eligible for refunds.

The cancellation drew significant attention on social media, with a video of Moroney's address to the Denver crowd circulating widely on TikTok.

topStory.headline: Musk's xAI Sues Minnesota Over First-in-Nation Law Banning AI Nudification Technology
topStory.summary:
Elon Musk's artificial intelligence company xAI filed a federal lawsuit Monday challenging a Minnesota law that bans so-called nudification technology — AI tools that generate fake nude images of real people. The suit was filed days before the law is set to take effect Saturday, making Minnesota the first state to attempt to outlaw such technology. The law, signed in May, imposes civil penalties of up to $500,000 per violation on companies whose platforms are used to create such images.

In its 38-page complaint, xAI said it does not dispute Minnesota's interest in preventing the non-consensual distribution of AI-generated nude images, but argues the law overreaches by restricting constitutionally protected speech. The company contends the statute lacks a safe harbor provision for platforms that make good-faith efforts to prevent misuse, that it applies even to images created or consented to by the depicted person, and that its definition of 'intimate part' is overly broad. Minnesota Attorney General Keith Ellison, who had not yet been served with the lawsuit, said in a statement that AI nudification 'robs the target of their dignity and can cause immense harm on an emotional, personal, and professional level.'

The legislation was authored in the state Senate by Democratic Sen. Erin Maye Quade, who said she began working on the bill two years ago after learning that a man had used social media photos of more than 80 women to generate hyperrealistic sexual images without their consent. The bill passed the state Senate unanimously and cleared the House with only one dissenting vote. Maye Quade said the law regulates conduct, not artistic content, and that no technology companies raised objections during the drafting process — with the exception of xAI.

Minnesota's law is distinct from existing state and federal statutes that penalize individuals who create and distribute non-consensual explicit deepfakes, as it targets the makers of the tools themselves. The federal Take It Down Act, passed last year, requires websites and apps to establish processes for removing such images but does not ban the underlying technology. Texas enacted a related but narrower law making platform owners liable if they knew an image was created without consent or failed to remove it promptly.

The case is expected to serve as a significant legal test of how far states can go in regulating AI under the First Amendment. State lawmakers note that similar legislation is advancing in more than a dozen other states, and a 2025 court challenge to the Minnesota law by Musk's company has so far failed. Ellison's office said it would review the lawsuit and respond accordingly.
